Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 1 Samuel 31, drawn from the sources I was able to consult within the available search and fetch limits.

---

## 1 Samuel 31 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1: "Now the Philistines fought against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before them, and many fell slain on Mount Gilboa."

**Traditional Reading**

The Philistines had advanced deep into Israelite territory, and Saul’s army assembled at Mount Gilboa (1 Sam 28:4). Saul, already in deep rebellion against the Lord, "was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly" (28:5). Instead of taking his fear to the Lord, Saul sought a spirit medium at Endor. There, through an extraordinary appearance of Samuel, he was told he and his sons would die the next day. 1 Samuel 31:1 *is* the next day (Guzik, Enduring Word).

The narrator’s style here is strikingly abrupt. Ellicott suggests this reflects the heart of a devoted patriot for whom "it was very bitter … to write the story of the fatal day of Gilboa." The historian returns to the battle "with evident reluctance" after the digression about David. The locale of the fight was likely the long vale at the foot of the hills occupied by the hostile camps; Israel was defeated and fled upward toward their old position on the slopes of Gilboa (Ellicott).

The Ligonier devotional stresses a key theological contrast: "God’s guidance and protection of David as recorded in 1 Samuel 29–30 stand in stark contrast to the fate of Saul described in chapter 31." Matthew Henry observed: "The very same day, perhaps, that David was triumphing over the Amalekites, were the Philistines triumphing over Saul. One is set over against the other, that men may see what comes of trusting in God and what comes of forsaking him" (Ligonier).

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saul-falls-to-philistines (excerpt via search)

### v. 2: "The Philistines followed hard after Saul and his sons, and they killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua."

**Traditional Reading**

The Philistines concentrated their attack on Saul and his sons. Tragically, Saul’s sons were caught up in the judgment of God against their father. Jonathan died as one would expect — loyally fighting for his God, his country, and his father to the very end (Guzik).

Matthew Poole saw a special providence in Jonathan’s death: "There was also a special providence of God in taking away Jonathan, (who of all Saul’s sons seems to have been the fairest for the crown,) for the preventing divisions, which have happened amongst the people concerning the successor; David’s way to the crown being by this means made the more clear" (Guzik, quoting Poole). God was also merciful to Jonathan, sparing him the ordeal of having to side with David against his own brothers.

Precept Austin notes that Saul "undoubtedly witnessed the slaying of his three sons," just as the priest Eli, though not physically present, heard of his sons' deaths at Philistine hands and died (1 Sam 4:18).

Ellicott observes that nothing is known of the two younger princes Abinadab and Malchishua. The three brothers likely "retreated (fighting all the while) to the hill of Gilboa … and there, no doubt defending the king to the last, they fell." Only Ish-bosheth (Eshbaal) survived and later became a rival king under Abner (2 Sam 2:8).

Dean Stanley is quoted by Ellicott: "The details of the battle are but seen in broken snatches … But amidst the showers of arrows from the Philistine archers, or pressed hard even on the mountain side by their charioteers, the figure of the king emerges from the darkness. His three sons have fallen before him."

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-31-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html

### v. 3: "When the battle intensified against Saul, the archers overtook him and wounded him critically."

**Traditional Reading**

After his sons fell, the battle focused on Saul himself. The great warrior-king fought fiercely, but his defenders fell one by one. Philistine archers — "shooters, men with bows, skilful shots" (margin reading) — were told off to target the towering figure of the king with the crown on his head (Ellicott).

Precept Austin stresses divine sovereignty even here: "The Philistine shot the arrow, but the LORD directed its course. This strike of Saul was not an accidental or chance hit." 1 Chronicles 10:14 states plainly: "Therefore He killed him and turned the kingdom to David the son of Jesse."

Ellicott notes a significant translation point: the more accurate rendering of the Hebrew is not "he was sore wounded" but **"he was sore afraid"** (so Gesenius, Keil, Lange, and others). Saul’s great courage finally failed him — his army routed, his sons dead, his faithful captains gone, archers shooting from a distance where his strong arm could not reach them, and Samuel's words from the night before ringing in his ears: "Tomorrow shalt thou and thy sons be with me." Gradually weakened through loss of blood, the undaunted courage at last failed (Ellicott).

Bible.org notes that none of Saul's arrow wounds were instantly fatal, but Saul knew "it is only a matter of time" (bible.org).

**Sources:**
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-31-commentary
- https://new.bible.org/seriespage/saul%E2%80%99s-death-wish-1-samuel-31

### v. 4: "Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, 'Draw your sword and run it through me, or these uncircumcised men will come and run me through and torture me!' But his armor-bearer was terrified and refused to do it. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it."

**Traditional Reading**

This is the central, most-discussed verse in the chapter. Saul, critically wounded and facing capture, commanded his armor-bearer to kill him. Guzik, following Adam Clarke, argues that "in the way most people think of suicide, Saul’s death was not suicide." Clarke wrote: "He was to all appearance mortally wounded, when he begged his armour bearer to extinguish the remaining spark of life … though this wound accelerated his death, yet it could not be properly the cause of it, as he was mortally wounded before." Guzik adds the sober observation that despite being told he would die the next day, Saul showed no repentance, no crying out to God, and no preparation of his soul to meet God (Guzik).

Precept Austin labels this "Saul seeks euthanasia." The writer notes Saul was focused on self to the very end — concerned with self-image — yet never cried out to Yahweh. Jewish tradition, cited by Precept Austin, holds that the armor-bearer was Doeg the Edomite, and that the sword Saul used was the same one with which Doeg had massacred the priests at Nob. If so, "Saul and his executioner fell by the same sword with which they massacred the priests of God."

Ellicott quotes Wordsworth on the irony of Saul’s dying words: "Even in Saul’s dying speech there is something of that religious formalism which marked his character after his fall from God, and which is a striking sign of spiritual blindness. He censures the Philistines as 'uncircumcised'" — yet his own heart was far from God. Ellicott also explains the physical act: Saul took the heavy war sword "from the reluctant hands of his faithful follower, and placing the hilt firmly on the ground, he threw the weight of his body on the point."

Bible.org draws attention to the parallel with Abimelech in Judges 9:54, who made the same request to avoid the disgrace of being killed by a woman. The armor-bearer refused, not necessarily out of principle (such as not touching the Lord's anointed) but "for he was greatly afraid" (bible.org).

**The Suicide Question — Differing Evaluations**

- **Guzik / Clarke (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Saul's act was not suicide in the normal sense; he was already dying; he merely accelerated the inevitable.

- **Precept Austin / Norman Geisler (Evangelical):** Saul committed suicide, a clear violation of the sixth commandment. "Suicide is murder, and the Bible says, 'You shall not murder' (Ex. 20:13). It makes no difference that the life taken is one’s own. All life belongs to God, and He alone has the right to take it." Scripture records at least five suicides (Abimelech, Saul, Zimri, Ahithophel, Judas), and none meets with divine approval. "Suicide is an attack on the image of God in man (Gen. 1:27) and an attempt to usurp God’s sovereignty over human life."

- **Bible.org (Evangelical):** Saul's death-wish was "one more attempt to disobey God, one final act of rebellion." He was wrong to try to alter the means of divine judgment. "Our text gives no sanction to assisted suicide."

- **G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Precept Austin):** "Suicide is always the ultimate action of cowardice. In the case of Saul, and in many similar cases, it is perfectly natural; but let it never be glorified as heroic."

- **Ellicott (Anglican, older):** Notes that theologians are divided on Saul's eternal fate. St. Bernard thought Saul was lost forever; Cornelius à Lapide and Bishop Wordsworth had no kindly thought for him. But Josephus "writes in warm and glowing terms of the patriotic devotion with which Saul went to meet his end." Many Rabbis sympathise with Josephus. Ellicott urges readers to imitate "the fearless human sympathy of the Biblical writers" and remember how David, the man after God's own heart, wrote his touching lament over Saul. "Without in any way justifying the fatal act … we may well plead in extenuation the awful position in which the king found himself."

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-31-commentary
- https://new.bible.org/seriespage/saul%E2%80%99s-death-wish-1-samuel-31
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html

### v. 5: "When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he too fell on his own sword and died with him."

**Traditional Reading**

The armor-bearer, seeing his king dead, took his own life. Precept Austin argues that the wording supports Saul actually being dead (not merely appearing so): "the text says Saul *was dead*. It does not say Saul *appeared to be* dead."

The question of the Amalekite’s alternate account in 2 Samuel 1:6–10 arises here. Did Saul die by his own hand or was he finished off by the Amalekite? Precept Austin concludes the Amalekite was lying to curry favor with David and "paid for his lie with his life." The writer notes: "There are no 'little' sins beloved!"

Ellicott, however, offers a harmonization: the armor-bearer, seeing the king pierced with arrows and falling on his sword, "may well have imagined his master dead, and so put an end to his own life. But Saul, though mortally wounded, may have rallied again for a brief space; in that brief space the Amalekite may have come up and finished the bloody work." Dean Stanley similarly pictures Saul receiving his death-blow, with "the dizziness and darkness of death … upon him," when "a wild Amalekite, lured probably to the field by the hope of spoil, came up and finished the work."

**Sources:**
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-31-commentary
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html

### v. 6: "So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that same day."

**Traditional Reading**

Guzik highlights the tragedy of what is absent: "As sad as anything was in this account, sad is the absence of any kind of sorrow or repentance or crying out to God at all on Saul’s part." Saul was told the day before that he would die, yet did not prepare his soul. Guzik warns: "Many people put off getting right with God until a later time, assuming they will still want to get right with God then. But that is a dangerous assumption because repentance is a gift from God."

F.B. Meyer is quoted: "It is a very solemn thought! No career could begin with fairer, brighter prospects than Saul had, and none could close in more absolute midnight of despair; and yet such a fate may befall us, unless we watch, and pray, and walk humbly with our God" (Guzik).

Ellicott clarifies that "all his men" is not absolutely literal. 1 Chronicles 10:6 says "all his house." Ish-bosheth and Abner survived; the meaning is that all of Saul's personal staff (*fideles*) fell fighting around him. Ellicott draws a parallel to the Scottish ballad of Flodden: "No one failed him! He is keeping / Royal state and semblance still, / Knight and noble lie around him, / Cold, on Flodden’s fatal hill."

G. Campbell Morgan, cited by Precept Austin, reflects: "This closing chapter of the Book is draped in sackcloth, and covered with ashes. It tells the tragic story of the last act in the career of a man who was a ghastly failure. … Suicide is always the ultimate action of cowardice."

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-31-commentary

### v. 7: "When the Israelites along the valley and those on the other side of the Jordan saw that the army of Israel had fled and that Saul and his sons had died, they abandoned their cities and ran away. So the Philistines came and occupied their cities."

**Traditional Reading**

The Philistine victory was so complete that Israelites on both sides of the Jordan — even those not directly in the path of the attack — panicked and fled. The Philistines occupied their abandoned cities, effectively cutting Israel in half (Guzik).

Guzik draws a leadership principle: "When the leader (King Saul) was struck, it spread panic among God's people." He links this to Jesus’ words in Mark 14:27: "I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered." Leaders carry a higher responsibility; the New Testament therefore sets a higher standard for them (1 Tim 3:2; Titus 1:6).

Ellicott explains the geography: "on the other side of the valley" means the land opposite the battlefield in the Jezreel Valley, occupied by Issachar, Zebulun, and Naphtali. "On the other side of Jordan" is the Transjordan. However, the Philistine penetration could not have been very deep east of the Jordan, since Abner soon rallied the house of Saul at Mahanaim, about twenty miles east of the river.

Bible.org makes an important theological point: "It is important to note here that Israel, as well as Saul, is being divinely disciplined." The people had demanded a king in 1 Samuel 8, rejecting God as their king (8:7–8). Samuel had warned in 1 Samuel 12:25: "If you still do wickedly, both you and your king shall be swept away." The national defeat was not only for Saul's sins but for Israel's collective sin of demanding a king like the nations (bible.org).

The Ligonier devotional adds that Saul's life ended in the exact opposite of his original calling: "The one whom God chose to defeat the Philistines was finally defeated by that same enemy (see 9:16). His fate shows that the Lord does not take persistent, impenitent disobedience lightly" (Ligonier, via search excerpt).

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html
- https://new.bible.org/seriespage/saul%E2%80%99s-death-wish-1-samuel-31
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saul-falls-to-philistines (search excerpt)

### vv. 8–9: "The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. They cut off Saul’s head, stripped off his armor, and sent messengers throughout the land of the Philistines to proclaim the news in the temples of their idols and among their people."

**Traditional Reading**

The Philistines only discovered the royal corpses on the morning after the battle — so fierce had been the fighting that night fell before the din of battle ceased. By then, the Amalekite had already taken the crown and royal bracelet (Ellicott).

Guzik notes the theological tragedy: "Saul’s tragic death gave an opportunity for the enemies of the Lord to disgrace His name. Saul’s death was used to glorify pagan gods and to mock the living God." The Philistines treated Saul's death as proof that their gods had triumphed over Yahweh.

Dr. Constable (Expository Notes, via search excerpt) notes a grim irony: "The Philistines cut off Saul’s head, as David had earlier cut off the head of Goliath, the Philistine champion (1 Sam 17:51)." David had taken Goliath's head to Jerusalem and put his weapons in his tent (later the tabernacle at Nob). Now the Philistines reciprocated. Constable also observes: "This book began with scenes from God’s temple, but it ends with scenes in the temples of Israel’s pagan enemies. David’s faith had brought Israel success, but Saul’s disobedience had lost it."

Bible.org stresses that Saul's two requests were both denied: he *was* killed by uncircumcised hands (both Philistine arrows and the Amalekite's sword), and he *was* made sport of. "A kind of poetic justice is described here. Saul is reaping what he himself has sewn. He is killed by uncircumcised hands because God said this was the way he would die. No matter how hard Saul tries to change his destiny, he cannot succeed at thwarting God’s will or His word" (bible.org).

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html
- https://new.bible.org/seriespage/saul%E2%80%99s-death-wish-1-samuel-31
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-31.html (search excerpt)

### v. 10: "They put his armor in the temple of the Ashtoreths and hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan."

**Traditional Reading**

"House of Ashtaroth" likely refers to the famous temple of Astarte (the Syrian Venus) at Askelon, described by Herodotus as the most ancient of the temples dedicated to her worship. This is corroborated by David's lament: "Proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon" (2 Sam 1:20). Alternatively, the plural "Ashtaroth" may indicate pieces of armor were distributed among various shrines (Ellicott).

Beth-shan was in the tribe of Manasseh, about four miles west of the Jordan and twelve miles south of the Sea of Galilee. Ellicott suggests the Philistines chose it because a Canaanite element still lived there (Judges 1:27), and "the Canaanites would probably have welcomed the miserable spectacle which seemed to degrade their ancient enemies." 1 Chronicles 10:10 adds the detail that Saul's skull was fastened in the temple of Dagon.

Guzik observes that in the ancient Near East, having your dead body treated this way was "considered a fate worse than death itself." He notes you can still visit the ruins of Beth-shan today, where the foundations sit high on a hill.

Constable explains: "In the ancient Near East the treatment of a corpse was very significant. If people, even enemies, honored a person, they treated his corpse with care … but if they did not respect him, they treated his dead body with contempt."

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-31.html (search excerpt)

### vv. 11–12: "When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, all their men of valor set out, journeyed all night, and retrieved the bodies of Saul and his sons from the wall of Beth-shan. When they arrived at Jabesh, they burned the bodies there."

**Traditional Reading**

This is the one bright light in an otherwise dark chapter. The men of Jabesh-gilead remembered that Saul's first act as king — his finest hour — was rescuing their city from Nahash the Ammonite (1 Samuel 11). Now, years later, they repaid that kindness. Guzik writes: "In a time of disgrace, loss, and tragedy like this, God still had valiant men to do His work." David later thanked these men for their kindness (2 Sam 2:4–7).

Ellicott explains that "burning the corpse was never the custom in Israel, and was restricted to criminals convicted of a crime of the deepest dye (Lev 20:14)." The reason here is practical: the mutilated bodies had been exposed for days, and the flesh was putrefied. Only the flesh was burned; the bones (v.13) were reverently preserved and buried. The Chaldee paraphrase interprets the burning as referring to the solemn burning of spices, a ceremony performed at the burials of some kings of Judah (2 Chron 16:14; 21:19; Jer 34:5), but Ellicott says the language here is different — "it is expressly stated that 'they burnt them.'"

Bible.org calculates this was "probably more than a 20-mile round trip" through the night — a courageous, dangerous mission into Philistine-occupied territory. It was Saul's first victory that saved Jabesh-gilead; now Jabesh-gilead's finest hour came in rescuing Saul's body.

The Pulpit Commentary (via search excerpt) extols the men of Jabesh-gilead: "It was … heroic and self-sacrificing; exhibited practically and at the risk of life, and displaying great energy and valour. 'The pillars of fire of genuine human heroism are the noble lights of history, which make us feel at ease while sojourning among spectres, and horrors, and graves' (Lange)."

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html
- https://new.bible.org/seriespage/saul%E2%80%99s-death-wish-1-samuel-31

### v. 13: "Then they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days."

**Traditional Reading**

The bones were buried under "the well-known tamarisk" (*êshel*) at Jabesh. Ellicott notes Saul's well-known love for trees (see 1 Sam 22:6, where Saul sat under a tamarisk at Gibeah), and the men of Jabesh-gilead "well remembered this peculiar fancy of their dead king, and under the waving branches of their own beautiful and famous tamarisk they tenderly laid the remains." Later, David had the remains moved to the family sepulchre of Kish, Saul's father, in Zelah of Benjamin (2 Sam 21:12–14).

The seven-day fast was the same period Israel mourned for Jacob (Gen 50:10). It was "mourning of the strictest kind." Ellicott adds that the Talmudic rule enjoining strict mourning for seven days was likely based on these two historic precedents — Jacob the patriarch and Saul the first king.

Guzik closes with the character of David: "When David heard of Saul’s death, he did not rejoice. In fact, he mourned and composed a song in honor of Saul and Jonathan (The Song of the Bow, 2 Sam 1:19–27). In spite of all that Saul did against David, David spoke well of Saul after his death." Choosing this kind of heart showed David to be a true man after God's own heart.

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-31-commentary

## Traditions Compared

### Reformed / Ligonier
The Reformed reading (represented by the Ligonier devotional) emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty in Saul's demise: Saul's death was God's doing (1 Chron 10:13–14). It interprets the chapter through the lens of covenant obedience — Saul proved to be "everything that the king of Israel should not be according to Deuteronomy 17:14–20." The juxtaposition of David's triumph (ch. 30) with Saul's defeat (ch. 31) teaches "what comes of trusting in God and what comes of forsaking him." Even in Saul's disgrace, however, God showed some grace: the men of Jabesh-gilead gave "the Lord's anointed" a proper burial. Ligonier also stresses that believers should not rejoice over the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11; David's lament as the model).

**Source:** https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/saul-falls-to-philistines (excerpts via search); https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/when-the-mighty-fall (excerpts via search)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik's reading is pastorally warm and emphasizes grace notes: Saul's death was not technically suicide (per Clarke); God mercifully spared Jonathan from having to choose between David and his brothers; God always has His "valiant men"; David's mourning shows how to be free from bitterness. The focus is on application to the believer's heart — repentance is a gift of God that must be received today, and "we should honor even those who opposed us once they are gone."

**Source:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-31/

### Evangelical / Bible.org
The Bible.org treatment foregrounds the moral issue of assisted suicide ("Dr. Jack Kevorkian") as a major contemporary application. It is the most explicit in condemning Saul's act as morally wrong: Saul was "attempting to minimize the pain of divine judgment," "attempting to alter the means of divine judgment," and trying "to kill the Lord's anointed." The Amalekite's account in 2 Samuel 1 is treated as a true report (Saul botched his suicide), making Saul's death a kind of dark comedy — "even here Saul cannot do it right."

**Source:** https://new.bible.org/seriespage/saul%E2%80%99s-death-wish-1-samuel-31

### Anglican / Older (Ellicott)
Ellicott's approach is literary and historically informed, showing deep sympathy for Saul while not justifying his act. It gives significant space to Jewish tradition (Doeg as armor-bearer), patristic and medieval opinions (Bernard vs. Josephus), and literary parallels (Dante, Browning, Aytoun, the Scottish ballad of Flodden). Ellicott urges readers to imitate "the fearless human sympathy of the Biblical writers" and to leave Saul "in the hands of his God." This tradition does not rush to declare Saul eternally lost and notes that David's inspired lament "dwells only on the Saul, the mighty conqueror, the delight of his people."

**Source:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-31.html

### Evangelical / Precept Austin
Precept Austin provides the most thorough treatment of the alleged contradiction between 1 Samuel 31 and 2 Samuel 1, citing Geisler, Kaiser, and Archer. The conclusion is firm: Saul committed suicide, and the Amalekite lied. Suicide is "an attack on the image of God in man" and "an attempt to usurp God's sovereignty over human life." None of the five biblical suicides meets with divine approval.

**Source:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-31-commentary
